metadata.author: Greg Paskal
metadata.description: X-Content-Type-Options header missing finding template with comprehensive guidance for all audiences including framework-specific implementation code, server configurations, and testing strategies to prevent MIME type sniffing attacks where browsers incorrectly interpret file content types, potentially executing malicious scripts disguised as benign content.

EXECUTIVE.summary: Your application lacks X-Content-Type-Options protection, allowing browsers to misinterpret file types and potentially execute malicious code disguised as safe content like images or text files.
EXECUTIVE.businessRisk: Low risk of MIME type sniffing attacks where browsers incorrectly interpret file content types. Attackers can exploit this to execute malicious scripts by uploading files with misleading extensions (e.g., JavaScript disguised as an image). Combined with file upload vulnerabilities, can lead to cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks. Lower priority than other security headers but part of defense-in-depth strategy. Minimal business impact if exploited, but contributes to overall security posture.
EXECUTIVE.complianceImpact: OWASP Top 10 A03:2021 (Injection) defense-in-depth control. CWE-16 (Configuration) and CWE-430 (Deployment of Wrong Handler) references. Some security frameworks and compliance audits check for presence of this header as part of baseline security controls. May appear in penetration test reports as informational or low-severity finding.

PROJECT_MANAGER.summary: Missing X-Content-Type-Options header allows browsers to guess file types, potentially enabling MIME sniffing attacks. Simple one-line fix with minimal risk.
PROJECT_MANAGER.timeline: Can be addressed in current or next sprint. Implementation takes 30 minutes to 1 hour including testing. Very low complexity change with no functional impact. Low priority unless combined with other vulnerabilities or required for compliance.
PROJECT_MANAGER.effort: 30 minutes to 1 hour for implementation and testing. Zero-risk change with no code modification.
dependencies: Access to web server or application configuration

DEVELOPER.summary: X-Content-Type-Options HTTP response header is not present, allowing browsers to perform MIME type sniffing, potentially executing malicious content with incorrect Content-Type headers.
DEVELOPER.technical: X-Content-Type-Options is an HTTP response header that prevents browsers from MIME-sniffing responses away from the declared Content-Type. Without this header, browsers (especially older versions of IE and Chrome) attempt to guess the content type by examining the content itself, ignoring the Content-Type header. This enables attacks where malicious JavaScript is uploaded as an image (image/jpeg) but executed as script. The header has one value: 'nosniff'. When set, browsers strictly follow the declared Content-Type and refuse to render content if mismatch detected. Particularly important for user-uploaded content, file downloads, and API responses. Supported by all modern browsers (IE8+, Chrome 1+, Firefox 50+, Safari 11+).
DEVELOPER.vulnerability: CWE-16 (Configuration) and CWE-430 (Deployment of Wrong Handler). MIME sniffing allows browsers to interpret files differently than server intended. Attack scenario: (1) Attacker uploads JavaScript file with .jpg extension, (2) Server returns it with Content-Type: image/jpeg, (3) Without X-Content-Type-Options, browser detects JavaScript and executes it, (4) XSS payload runs in victim's browser. Also exploitable in: CSS files containing JavaScript, HTML files disguised as text, SVG files with embedded scripts. Most effective when combined with file upload vulnerabilities or user-generated content.

SECURITY_ENGINEER.summary: Missing X-Content-Type-Options enables MIME type sniffing attacks where browsers execute malicious content by ignoring declared Content-Type headers, creating XSS attack vectors.
SECURITY_ENGINEER.vulnerability: CWE-16 (Configuration), CWE-430 (Deployment of Wrong Handler). MIME sniffing exploits browser behavior of content type detection. Without X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, browsers examine file content to determine type, overriding server-declared Content-Type. Attack vectors: (1) Upload JavaScript disguised as image, (2) Inject script into CSS files, (3) Upload HTML as plain text, (4) SVG files with embedded JavaScript, (5) Polyglot files valid as multiple types. Most dangerous with file upload features or user-generated content hosting.
SECURITY_ENGINEER.attackVector: Attacker uploads malicious file with misleading extension/Content-Type. Examples: JavaScript with .jpg extension and Content-Type: image/jpeg, HTML with .txt extension and Content-Type: text/plain, SVG with embedded script. Browser performs MIME sniffing, detects actual content type (JavaScript/HTML), executes code despite incorrect Content-Type header. Results in XSS, data theft, session hijacking. Requires file upload capability or ability to influence server-served content. Effectiveness reduced in modern browsers but still exploitable, especially in legacy browser support scenarios.
SECURITY_ENGINEER.threatLevel: LOW - Modern browsers have improved MIME sniffing protections, reducing attack surface. However, defense-in-depth principle recommends implementation. Critical for applications with: file upload features, user-generated content, legacy browser support, untrusted content serving. Combined with other vulnerabilities (file upload bypass, insufficient validation), severity increases to MEDIUM. Simple fix with no performance impact makes implementation worthwhile despite low base risk.
SECURITY_ENGINEER.mitigationUrgency: Implement within 1-4 weeks as part of security header hardening. Can be bundled with other security header implementations (CSP, X-Frame-Options, HSTS). Higher priority (1-2 weeks) if application allows file uploads or serves user-generated content. Very low implementation complexity with zero functional risk.

OPS_INFRASTRUCTURE.summary: Web servers not configured to send X-Content-Type-Options header, requiring simple HTTP response header configuration across infrastructure.
OPS_INFRASTRUCTURE.technical: X-Content-Type-Options header must be added to HTTP responses at web server, reverse proxy, or application layer. Header syntax: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff (only valid value). Typically configured in Nginx, Apache, load balancers, CDN, or application middleware. Simple one-line configuration change. Should be applied globally to all responses. No performance impact. Works in conjunction with proper Content-Type headers on all resources.
OPS_INFRASTRUCTURE.scope: All web servers serving application traffic: production web servers, load balancers, CDN origin shields, API gateways, reverse proxies. Must be consistent across all environments (dev, staging, production). Applies to all HTTP responses including: HTML pages, API responses, static assets (CSS, JS, images), file downloads, user-uploaded content.
OPS_INFRASTRUCTURE.monitoring: Monitor for correct Content-Type headers on all resources. Verify X-Content-Type-Options present using security scanners. Use browser DevTools to verify header in responses. No specific runtime monitoring needed - header presence is static configuration. Include in regular security header audits.

QA_TESTER.summary: Missing X-Content-Type-Options header prevents validation that browsers strictly respect declared Content-Type headers and block MIME sniffing attacks.
QA_TESTER.testImplication: Cannot validate MIME sniffing prevention controls. Security testing tools (Burp Suite, OWASP ZAP) flag missing X-Content-Type-Options as low-severity finding. After implementation, must test: (1) Header present on all responses, (2) Application functionality unaffected, (3) File uploads and downloads work correctly, (4) No Content-Type mismatches causing browser errors.
QA_TESTER.riskIfNotFixed: Security audit finding (informational/low severity). Penetration test report item. Incomplete defense-in-depth security posture. Potential MIME sniffing exploitation if combined with file upload vulnerabilities. Modern browsers less affected but legacy browser support remains vulnerable.

django-python.code:
# Django - Add X-Content-Type-Options via settings
# settings.py

# Method 1: Use Django's built-in SecurityMiddleware
MIDDLEWARE = [
    'django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware',  # Includes X-Content-Type-Options
    # ... other middleware
]

# Enable secure content type sniffing prevention
SECURE_CONTENT_TYPE_NOSNIFF = True

# Method 2: Custom middleware for more control
# middleware.py
class SecurityHeadersMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response
    
    def __call__(self, request):
        response = self.get_response(request)
        
        # Set X-Content-Type-Options header
        response['X-Content-Type-Options'] = 'nosniff'
        
        # Also add other security headers
        response['X-Frame-Options'] = 'DENY'
        response['X-XSS-Protection'] = '1; mode=block'
        
        return response

# Add custom middleware to MIDDLEWARE list
# MIDDLEWARE = [
#     'your_app.middleware.SecurityHeadersMiddleware',
#     # ... other middleware
# ]

# Method 3: Using django-csp package (includes X-Content-Type-Options)
# Install: pip install django-csp
# MIDDLEWARE = [
#     'csp.middleware.CSPMiddleware',
#     # ...
# ]
# CSP_DEFAULT_SRC = ("'self'",)

# Method 4: Per-view decorator (not recommended - use global setting)
from django.views.decorators.http import require_safe

def add_security_headers(view_func):
    def wrapper(request, *args, **kwargs):
        response = view_func(request, *args, **kwargs)
        response['X-Content-Type-Options'] = 'nosniff'
        return response
    return wrapper

@add_security_headers
def my_view(request):
    return HttpResponse('Protected view')

generic.code:
# Generic X-Content-Type-Options Implementation Guidelines

## Header Syntax

X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

# This is the ONLY valid value for this header
# There are no other options or directives

## What It Does

1. Prevents browsers from MIME-sniffing responses
2. Forces browsers to respect the Content-Type header
3. Blocks execution if Content-Type mismatches actual content

## Implementation Locations

### Application Level (Recommended)
- Add header in application middleware/framework
- Benefits: Consistent across all responses, version controlled
- See framework examples above

### Web Server Level
- Add header in Nginx/Apache/IIS configuration
- Benefits: No application code changes needed
- See server configuration examples below

### CDN/Load Balancer Level
- Add header at edge or load balancer
- Benefits: Applies to all origin content
- See AWS CloudFront example below

## When to Apply

Apply X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff to:
- ✅ All HTML pages
- ✅ All API responses (JSON, XML, etc.)
- ✅ All static assets (CSS, JS, images)
- ✅ All file downloads
- ✅ User-uploaded content
- ✅ Error pages (4xx, 5xx)

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ Don't use any value other than "nosniff"
❌ Don't conditionally apply (should be global)
❌ Don't forget error responses
❌ Don't rely on browser defaults

## Best Practices

✅ Apply globally to all responses
✅ Set correct Content-Type headers on all resources
✅ Test with different file types
✅ Include in security header policy
✅ Combine with CSP for defense-in-depth

## Browser Compatibility

- Internet Explorer 8+
- Chrome 1+
- Firefox 50+
- Safari 11+
- Edge (all versions)

## Testing

Verify header present:
curl -I https://your-domain.com | grep -i x-content-type-options

Expected output:
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
generic.testCode:
# Generic X-Content-Type-Options Testing

## Browser DevTools Testing

1. Open browser DevTools (F12)
2. Go to Network tab
3. Navigate to your site
4. Click on any request (HTML, CSS, JS, API)
5. Go to Headers section
6. Look for X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff in Response Headers

## Command-Line Testing

# Check if header is present
curl -I https://your-domain.com | grep -i x-content-type-options

# Expected output:
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

# Test multiple resources
for path in / /api/data /style.css /script.js; do
  echo "Testing $path:"
  curl -I https://your-domain.com$path | grep -i x-content-type-options
done

# Test different HTTP methods
curl -I -X GET https://your-domain.com/api/data | grep -i x-content
curl -I -X POST https://your-domain.com/api/data | grep -i x-content

## MIME Sniffing Test

# Create test file that could be MIME-sniffed
# Example: JavaScript served as text/plain

1. Create file: test.txt containing JavaScript:
   alert('XSS');

2. Serve with incorrect Content-Type: text/plain

3. Try to execute in browser:
   <script src="/test.txt"></script>

4. With X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff:
   - Browser blocks execution
   - Console shows: "Refused to execute script because MIME type mismatch"

5. Without header:
   - Browser might execute (MIME sniffing)
   - Alert appears (security risk)

## Online Testing Tools

1. Security Headers Scanner
   https://securityheaders.com/
   - Enter your domain
   - Verify X-Content-Type-Options present

2. Mozilla Observatory
   https://observatory.mozilla.org/
   - Comprehensive security scan
   - Checks X-Content-Type-Options

3. SSL Labs
   https://www.ssllabs.com/ssltest/
   - HTTP header analysis

## Automated Testing Script

#!/bin/bash
# test-xcto.sh

URL="$1"

if [ -z "$URL" ]; then
  echo "Usage: $0 <url>"
  exit 1
fi

echo "Testing X-Content-Type-Options for: $URL"

XCTO=$(curl -s -I "$URL" | grep -i "^x-content-type-options:" | cut -d: -f2 | tr -d '\r\n ')

if [ -z "$XCTO" ]; then
  echo "❌ X-Content-Type-Options header is MISSING"
  exit 1
else
  echo "✅ X-Content-Type-Options: $XCTO"
  
  if [ "$XCTO" == "nosniff" ]; then
    echo "✅ Correct value (nosniff)"
  else
    echo "❌ Incorrect value - should be 'nosniff'"
  fi
fi

# Test multiple resource types
echo ""
echo "Testing different resource types:"

for path in / /api/data /static/style.css /static/script.js; do
  RESULT=$(curl -s -I "$URL$path" | grep -i "^x-content-type-options:")
  if [ -n "$RESULT" ]; then
    echo "✅ $path"
  else
    echo "❌ $path - header missing"
  fi
done

apache.config:
# Apache - Add X-Content-Type-Options header
# /etc/apache2/sites-available/your-site.conf or .htaccess

<VirtualHost *:443>
    ServerName your-domain.com
    
    # Enable mod_headers if not enabled
    # a2enmod headers
    
    # Add X-Content-Type-Options header
    Header always set X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff"
    
    # Other recommended security headers
    Header always set X-Frame-Options "DENY"
    Header always set X-XSS-Protection "1; mode=block"
    Header always set Referrer-Policy "strict-origin-when-cross-origin"
    Header always set Content-Security-Policy "default-src 'self'"
    
    DocumentRoot /var/www/html
    
    <Directory /var/www/html>
        Options -Indexes +FollowSymLinks
        AllowOverride All
        Require all granted
    </Directory>
    
    SSLEngine on
    SSLCertificateFile /etc/ssl/certs/your-cert.crt
    SSLCertificateKeyFile /etc/ssl/private/your-key.key
</VirtualHost>

# Alternative: .htaccess file
<IfModule mod_headers.c>
  Header always set X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff"
</IfModule>

OPS_INFRASTRUCTURE.rollbackPlan:
1. Keep backup of current configuration files
2. Document current header configuration
3. If X-Content-Type-Options causes issues (extremely rare), remove header
4. For Nginx: Comment out header line, test with 'nginx -t', reload
5. For Apache: Comment out header line, test with 'apachectl configtest', reload
6. For AWS CloudFront: Remove X-Content-Type-Options from Response Headers Policy
7. Verify application functionality restored
8. Investigate root cause (usually incorrect Content-Type headers on resources)
9. Fix Content-Type headers on affected resources
10. Re-deploy X-Content-Type-Options header
